# Treatment limitation documentation confounds risk-adjusted mortality benchmarking in intensive care: an analysis of 136,236 admissions across 190 US hospitals

**Draft v1 — 2026-08-06.** All numbers generated by `R/01`–`R/07` from
`data_private/analytic.csv`. Target: *Annals of the American Thoracic Society*.

---

## Abstract

**Rationale.** Standardised mortality ratios (SMRs) derived from severity-of-illness
scores are widely used to compare intensive care unit performance. These scores predict
mortality under full treatment and do not incorporate treatment-limitation decisions.
If hospitals differ in how often they document such limitations for reasons unrelated to
their patients, SMR-based comparisons may reflect end-of-life practice rather than
quality of care.

**Objective.** To determine whether between-hospital variation in treatment-limitation
documentation reflects patient case-mix or local practice, and to quantify its
consequences for risk-adjusted mortality benchmarking.

**Methods.** Retrospective analysis of 136,236 adult ICU admissions with APACHE IVa
predictions across 190 US hospitals in the eICU Collaborative Research Database
(2014–2015). Treatment limitation within 24 hours of admission was classified on an
ordered scale from full therapy to comfort measures only. We assessed APACHE IVa
calibration within limitation strata, estimated between-hospital variation before and
after case-mix adjustment using mixed-effects models, and compared hospital rankings
computed with and without accounting for limitation status.

**Measurements and Main Results.** Code status was documented in 96.1% of admissions;
9.9% had a limitation within 24 hours. APACHE IVa calibration slope was 1.005 with
intercept −0.425, indicating uniform over-prediction. SMR rose monotonically across
limitation strata, from 0.61 under full therapy to 1.89 under comfort measures only,
and the integrated calibration index was 7–9 times larger in the comfort-measures
stratum (0.34) than in any other (0.04–0.05). Between-hospital variation in limitation
documentation was **not** attenuated by case-mix adjustment (ICC 0.084 unadjusted vs
0.104 adjusted; median odds ratio 1.69 vs 1.80), with a 4.8-fold difference between the
5th and 95th percentile hospitals after adjustment. Incorporating limitation status into
risk adjustment changed hospital quartile assignment for 23.5% of hospitals and reversed
mortality-outlier classification for 8.0%; the direction of movement was strongly
predicted by a hospital's limitation rate (Spearman ρ = −0.689, p = 3.7×10⁻²⁴). Simply
excluding the 0.6% of admissions under comfort-measures orders reclassified 11.1% of
hospitals across quartiles.

**Conclusions.** Hospitals differ several-fold in how often they document treatment
limitation, and this variation is not explained by their patients. Because severity
scores do not account for these decisions, SMR-based ICU benchmarking systematically
disadvantages hospitals that document limitations more often. Excluding admissions under
comfort-measures orders is a simple partial remedy.

---

## Introduction

*[~500 words. Structure:]*

1. SMRs from APACHE, SAPS and similar scores are the standard currency of ICU
   benchmarking, used in registries, quality programmes and payer comparisons.
2. These models are estimated on populations receiving full treatment and contain no
   term for treatment limitation. A do-not-resuscitate order or transition to comfort
   care changes the probability of death without changing physiology.
3. Prior work has shown these scores over-predict in contemporary cohorts
   (Feng & Dubin 2021 report predicted 11.96% vs observed 9.91% in eICU) and
   under-perform in specific subgroups, but has treated miscalibration as a property of
   the score or the patient rather than of the care plan.
4. Hospital-level variation in end-of-life practice is well described, and has been
   *hypothesised* to contribute to variation in ICU utilisation (Hart et al. 2014,
   a simulation study). Whether it distorts risk-adjusted mortality comparisons has not
   been tested empirically.
5. **Objective**, as stated above.

## Methods

### Data source and cohort

eICU-CRD v2.0, comprising 200,859 ICU stays at 208 US hospitals participating in a
tele-critical-care programme during 2014–2015. We included adult unit stays with a valid
APACHE IVa predicted hospital mortality (`apacheversion = 'IVa'`,
predicted mortality > 0) linked to the APACHE predictor table, yielding **136,236 stays
at 190 hospitals**. Hospital-level analyses were restricted to the **162 hospitals with
≥100 stays**.

### Exposure

Treatment limitation was taken from structured care-plan documentation
(`careplangeneral`, group "Care Limitation"). For each stay we took the most restrictive
value recorded within 24 hours of unit admission, on an ordered scale:

| Tier | Definition | n | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| Undocumented | no entry | 5,363 | 3.9 |
| 1 | Full therapy | 117,377 | 86.2 |
| 2 | DNR-type — do not resuscitate, no CPR, no intubation, no cardioversion | 11,929 | 8.8 |
| 3 | Partial withdrawal — no vasopressors, no augmentation, no blood products/draws | 689 | 0.5 |
| 4 | Comfort measures only | 878 | 0.6 |

### Outcome

In-hospital mortality, compared against APACHE IVa predicted hospital mortality.

### Statistical analysis

**Calibration.** Logistic recalibration, regressing observed mortality on the logit of
predicted mortality; a slope of 1 and intercept of 0 indicate perfect calibration.
Calibration within strata was summarised by SMR and by the integrated calibration index
(ICI), the mean absolute difference between a loess-smoothed observed risk and predicted
risk. Standard errors were clustered on hospital throughout.

**Practice versus case-mix.** Between-hospital variation in limitation documentation was
estimated with mixed-effects logistic models with a hospital random intercept, before
and after adjustment for the APACHE linear predictor, age, sex, malignancy,
immunosuppression, cirrhosis, diabetes and day-1 ventilation. Variation was expressed as
the intraclass correlation coefficient and the median odds ratio.

**Benchmarking impact.** Expected deaths per hospital were computed two ways: from a
recalibrated APACHE IVa model (current practice), and from a model additionally
containing limitation status. Hospitals were ranked by SMR under each and compared on
rank shift, quartile change, and outlier status using exact Poisson 95% limits. We
additionally compared two simpler strategies: excluding comfort-measures admissions, and
excluding all admissions with any limitation.

**Discrimination.** Assessed on a random 30% hold-out (n = 40,871) by area under the ROC
curve with DeLong's test, and Brier score.

Analyses used R 4.6.0. Code is available at *[repository]*.

## Results

### Cohort

Of 136,236 admissions, mean APACHE IVa predicted mortality was 11.8% against observed
mortality of 8.85% (**SMR 0.75**). Code status was documented within 24 hours in
**96.1%** of admissions — a near-universal field. A limitation beyond full therapy was
present in **9.9%**.

*[Table 1 — cohort characteristics, from `results/table1_cohort.csv`]*

### APACHE IVa calibration depends on treatment limitation

Overall calibration slope was **1.005** with intercept **−0.425**: the score ranks
patients essentially perfectly but is uniformly shifted, over-predicting death across the
whole risk range.

Calibration differed sharply by limitation status:

| Code status | n | Predicted | Observed | SMR | ICI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full therapy | 117,377 | 10.5% | 6.5% | **0.61** | 0.039 |
| DNR-type | 11,929 | 22.3% | 26.1% | **1.17** | 0.037 |
| Partial withdrawal | 689 | 26.2% | 32.1% | **1.22** | 0.054 |
| Comfort measures only | 878 | 39.6% | 74.1% | **1.89** | **0.34** |

In a recalibration model with full therapy as reference, the adjusted odds of death were
2.63 (95% CI 2.45–2.83) for DNR-type, 2.97 (2.19–4.02) for partial withdrawal and
**15.30 (12.14–19.29)** for comfort measures only. Adding limitation status reduced
model deviance by 3.6%, compared with 0.0% for malignancy.

On held-out data, adding limitation status improved discrimination from AUC 0.8657 to
**0.8760** (DeLong p < 2.2×10⁻¹⁶) and reduced Brier score from 0.0621 to 0.0579.

### Between-hospital variation is practice, not case-mix

Across 162 hospitals, limitation rates ranged from **0% to 27.5%** (median 10.5%,
IQR 7.5–14.5%).

Case-mix adjustment did **not** attenuate this variation:

| | Unadjusted | Case-mix adjusted |
|---|---|---|
| ICC | 0.084 | **0.104** |
| Median odds ratio | 1.69 | **1.80** |

126% of the between-hospital variance survived adjustment. Comparing observed with
case-mix-expected limitation rates, hospitals differed **4.8-fold** between the 5th and
95th percentiles; one hospital documented no limitations at all across more than 100
admissions.

### Consequences for benchmarking

Incorporating limitation status into risk adjustment left the overall ranking broadly
similar (Spearman ρ = 0.949) but moved individual hospitals substantially: median
absolute shift **7.5 positions** of 162, with 38.3% moving more than 10 positions and
14.8% more than 20.

- **23.5%** of hospitals changed quartile
- **8.0%** changed mortality-outlier classification: four hospitals previously flagged as
  high-mortality became "as expected", and three previously unflagged became outliers

Movement was systematic, not random. Signed rank shift correlated strongly with a
hospital's limitation rate (ρ = **−0.689**, p = 3.7×10⁻²⁴):

| Limitation-rate quintile | Mean rate | SMR, current | SMR, adjusted | Mean rank shift |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 5.1% | 0.984 | **1.027** | +12.7 |
| Q2 | 8.1% | 0.992 | 1.006 | +6.9 |
| Q3 | 10.5% | 0.993 | 0.976 | +0.7 |
| Q4 | 13.6% | 0.995 | 0.931 | −4.5 |
| Q5 | 19.0% | 1.013 | **0.876** | −15.7 |

Under current benchmarking all five quintiles appear equivalent (0.984–1.013). Once
limitation status is accounted for they separate from 1.027 to 0.876.

### A simpler remedy

| Strategy | Admissions affected | Hospitals changing quartile |
|---|---|---|
| Exclude comfort-measures only | **0.6%** (878) | **11.1%** |
| Adjust for full limitation scale | 0% | 23.5% |
| Exclude any limitation | 9.9% | 28.4% |

Excluding 878 of 136,236 admissions — six in every thousand — reclassified 18 of 162
hospitals across mortality quartiles.

## Discussion

*[~800 words. Points to make:]*

1. **Principal finding.** Hospitals differ several-fold in limitation documentation, none
   of it explained by case-mix, and this materially changes benchmarking outcomes.
2. **Mechanism.** Severity scores estimate mortality under full treatment by
   construction. They are therefore valid only where that assumption holds, and the
   assumption fails in 9.9% of admissions and collapses entirely in 0.6%.
3. **This is a choice, not an error.** Whether to adjust for limitation status is
   genuinely contested. Adjusting treats it as patient preference and case-mix; not
   adjusting treats it as a modifiable hospital behaviour. Adjusting for a hospital's own
   decision risks masking premature withdrawal. **We do not claim adjustment is correct —
   we show the choice is consequential and currently made by default, without
   examination.**
4. **Comparison with prior work.** Feng & Dubin (2021) found APACHE IVa over-prediction in
   eICU and included limitation *change frequency* among predictors of classification
   error, but did not examine calibration or benchmarking. Hart et al. (2014) hypothesised
   that advance-care-planning norms drive variation in ICU utilisation, by simulation;
   we provide the empirical test in a benchmarking context.
5. **Clinical implication.** Excluding comfort-measures admissions is simple,
   affects 0.6% of the denominator, and recovers roughly half the effect.
6. **Limitations** — see below.

### Limitations

1. Documentation is not practice: we observe charting, not decisions or the care
   delivered. Hospitals may limit treatment without recording it, which would
   *understate* true variation.
2. Data are from 2014–2015 and from US ICUs participating in a single tele-critical-care
   programme; generalisability to other systems and eras is untested.
3. Limitation status is partly a *consequence* of prognosis. Clinicians write these
   orders because they expect death, so limitation encodes prognostic information the
   score lacks; associations must not be read causally.
4. Adjusting for limitation status is adjustment for a variable partly under hospital
   control, with the mediator-adjustment hazards that implies.
5. eICU contains only participating ICUs, not a census of each hospital's activity.
6. Cancer ascertainment from APACHE comorbidity flags captures metastatic solid tumour
   and haematologic malignancy only; agreement with diagnosis-based ascertainment was
   poor (1,906 of 5,465 diagnosis-identified stays also flagged).

## Conclusion

Hospitals vary several-fold in how often they document treatment limitation, and that
variation is not explained by the patients they treat. Because severity-of-illness scores
assume full treatment, risk-adjusted mortality benchmarking systematically disadvantages
hospitals that document limitations more frequently. Excluding admissions under
comfort-measures orders — six per thousand — reclassifies one hospital in nine.
